title: 33 Max Verstappen
blurb: Number 33 was Verstappen's racing number before he became champion, and a Dutch dance track turned it into a chant. Carte Blanq and Maxx Power built the song around commentary and snatches of onboard team radio, then put it online in 2022, a couple of months after he won his first title. TikTok found it the following year and gave it one job: soundtracking anybody who needs to be somewhere immediately. Late for a lecture, sprinting for a train, leaving a party without saying goodbye. It helps that the track genuinely does sound like acceleration.
origin: From the 2022 track '33 Max Verstappen' by Carte Blanq and Maxx Power, built around Verstappen commentary and team radio.

title: Aguerooo
blurb: Stoppage time at the Etihad, 13 May 2012, and Manchester City needed one more goal to take the Premier League from Manchester United on goal difference. Sergio Aguero supplied it with practically the last kick of the season. What you can hear afterwards is a commentator abandoning composure completely, holding the striker's name until his lungs give out — a reaction nobody could fake, which is why the clip still travels. English football had not had a finish like it. Reach for it after any rescue that arrives far too late to be sensible.
origin: Television commentary on Sergio Aguero's title-winning goal for Manchester City against QPR, 13 May 2012.

title: Cell Phone Ringing
blurb: Ten seconds of a phone demanding attention, unbranded and entirely unhurried. No handset maker owns this one, which makes it the ring of choice for films, stage plays and student videos that cannot afford to licence anything Apple made. It also makes an excellent nuisance. Play it quietly in an open-plan office and watch four people pat their pockets at once. Sound designers keep a version on hand because a ringing phone interrupts a scene faster than almost anything else — somebody is calling, nobody knows who, and nothing continues until it gets answered.
origin: A generic mobile phone ringing tone.

title: Cingular AT&T Ringtone
blurb: Americans on Cingular heard this constantly, back when a carrier could still stamp its identity onto the handset itself. Cingular took the AT&T name in 2007 and the orange jack logo vanished, but the ringtone outlived the brand the way these things tend to. It turns up now in edits about the mid-2000s, filed alongside flip phones and nights-and-weekends minutes. There is no melody here worth humming. It is a chirpy little pattern engineered to cut through a coat pocket in a noisy room, and it does that job perfectly well.
origin: The ringtone associated with Cingular Wireless handsets, before the carrier was rebranded as AT&T in 2007.

title: Dial-Up Sound
blurb: Six seconds is the polite version. A real 56k connection took the better part of a minute to shriek its way to a working link, and every stage of it came out of the modem's own speaker so you could tell by ear whether things were going wrong. Editors now use the noise as instant shorthand for the past, the way a rotary dial or a VHS tracking line works. Anyone under twenty-five hears an alien transmission. Anyone older hears a sibling picking up the phone downstairs and killing the whole thing stone dead.
origin: The handshake tones of a dial-up modem connecting over a telephone line.

title: Encara Messi
blurb: Catalan radio commentary from April 2007, recorded while Messi ran most of Getafe's defence out of the picture and finished a goal people still measure against Maradona. The commentator repeats his name in rising disbelief, and because the delivery is fast and the accent unfamiliar to most of the internet, English speakers heard Ankara instead of the Catalan word. Ankara Messi stuck — a mishearing now far better known than the phrase it mangled. TikTok layered it over a dreamy remix in 2021 and the clip escaped football entirely. Plenty of those videos contain no ball at all.
origin: Catalan radio commentary on Lionel Messi's solo goal against Getafe in April 2007.

title: Goal Horn
blurb: Three seconds of blaring air horn, the noise an arena makes the instant the home side scores. Ice hockey rinks made the tradition famous and football clubs borrowed it, each one guarding its own horn as jealously as its crest. The function is simple and slightly primal: it tells a building full of thousands to make noise now, and the building obeys. Nothing about it is musical. Drop it on any small victory deserving of disproportionate celebration, such as landing a parallel park first time or finding money you had written off.
origin: A stadium goal horn, the type sounded in arenas when the home team scores.

title: Goalllll
blurb: Held for as long as one set of lungs allows, this is the elongated goal call that Latin American broadcasting turned into a discipline. Length grades the moment. A routine tap-in earns a short one; a decisive strike gets an aria, and the commentator's stamina becomes part of the record. Spanish-language television carried the style to the rest of the world, and it long ago escaped football, turning up over exam results, job offers and successfully reversed trailers. No subtlety is available here and none is wanted. Fair warning that this clip runs much longer than most soundboard buttons.
origin: An extended 'goooool' call in the Latin American football commentary tradition.

title: Harry Maguire
blurb: Under two seconds, just the England defender's name, shouted. Maguire became a reliable engine of football memes over the course of his career, partly because he is enormous and partly because the internet decided every clip of him arrived pre-funny. Where this particular shout was recorded is genuinely unclear; it has circulated on soundboards for years with no reliable source attached to it. The appeal is the same as a name yelled across a crowded pub, which is to say instant and requiring no explanation. Best deployed on anyone tall who has just done something clumsy.
origin: A short shout of the footballer Harry Maguire's name, widely circulated as a soundboard clip.

title: Hello There (Obi-Wan)
blurb: Obi-Wan drops several storeys, lands in front of General Grievous, and greets him like a neighbour over a garden fence. Revenge of the Sith gave the line its delivery in 2005, though Alec Guinness had already said the same two words to Artoo back in 1977, a callback most people discover long afterwards. Prequel memes did the rest. Post it anywhere online and somebody will reply General Kenobi within a minute, unprompted, as though contractually obliged to. Ideal for entering a Discord call you were not strictly invited to.
origin: Obi-Wan Kenobi's greeting to General Grievous in Star Wars: Revenge of the Sith (2005), echoing Alec Guinness's line in A New Hope (1977).

title: Mbappe Special
blurb: Asked in a 2026 interview what he likes to cook, Mbappe thought about it and answered: nothing. The clip travelled fast, and the phrase turned into internet shorthand for an empty answer, an empty fridge, an empty bank balance. Half the appeal is the delivery, which is completely unbothered. Footballers are usually media-trained into producing something, anything, and he simply declined to. Caption a photograph of nothing at all with this and the joke lands without further work. Rare among football memes in requiring no knowledge of football whatsoever.
origin: From a 2026 interview in which Kylian Mbappe was asked what he cooks and answered 'nothing'.

title: Nintendo Switch Click
blurb: Slide a Joy-Con down the rail and the Switch answers with this. Nintendo's designers liked how magnets snapped together and engineered the mechanical rail specifically to keep that feeling, so the click does two jobs at once: locking the controller in place, and confirming to your hands that it locked. The 2017 reveal trailer leaned on the noise heavily, which is how a fraction of a second ended up standing in for an entire console. Under a second long and weirdly moreish. People detach and reattach controllers purely to hear it again.
origin: The click of a Joy-Con attaching to the Nintendo Switch console (2017).

title: Shooting Stars
blurb: Bag Raiders put this out in 2009 and it did modest business, an Australian electro track with a chorus built for driving at night. Then in early 2017 somebody paired it with footage of a man falling, edited so that he tumbled off into a starfield. The format ran for months. Anybody stumbling, jumping badly or losing their footing got the same treatment. The song became inseparable from the joke — to the mild bemusement of the duo who wrote it. Years later, people still cannot hear the intro without expecting somebody to drop out of frame.
origin: 'Shooting Stars' by Australian duo Bag Raiders, released as a single in 2009 and turned into a falling-video meme in early 2017.

title: Star Wars Theme
blurb: Brass in the key of triumph, written by John Williams and recorded with the London Symphony Orchestra for the 1977 opening crawl. Williams was deliberately old-fashioned about the score, borrowing the sweep of Golden Age Hollywood at a point when film music had largely moved on to synthesisers and pop songs. That choice is why the theme still sounds enormous rather than dated. Forty seconds in, most listeners are sitting slightly straighter — the fanfare does not ask for attention, it instructs. Use it for entrances and reveals. It will make any announcement sound considerably more important than it actually is.
origin: The main title theme from Star Wars (1977), composed by John Williams and recorded by the London Symphony Orchestra.

title: Wii Shop Channel Music
blurb: Kazumi Totaka wrote this jaunty little loop for the Wii Shop Channel, which opened in late 2006 and closed for good in 2019. Its job was to keep you company while you converted real money into Wii Points and watched a download meter crawl. Somehow it became one of the most remixed pieces of music on the internet, spawning years of joke arrangements in every genre going. The tune is far better than it ever needed to be. Totaka has form for that, having quietly hidden a nineteen-note signature melody in Nintendo games for decades.
origin: The background music of the Nintendo Wii Shop Channel (2006-2019), composed by Kazumi Totaka.

title: WWE Ring Bell
blurb: Ding ding ding. In wrestling the bell is the one honest object in the building: it starts the match, ends the match, and rings the instant somebody taps out or cannot answer the count. Everything else is choreography. Promotions also ring it ten deliberate times as a memorial for a wrestler who has died, a tradition WWE has observed since at least the early nineties, so the sound carries weight it has no obvious right to. On a soundboard it works as a full stop — end of round, end of argument, end of discussion.
origin: The ring bell used in professional wrestling to start and end matches.
